catalog_quote: The Kayah Li* phonological word is the structure of those lexical items which are neither analyzeable compounds; truly polysyllabic morphemes ...; nor suspect polysyllabic morphemes ... This structure may be abbreviated as: 1) t T t / c v C C V v. Upper-case elements are required, and lower-case are optional ... CCV is main syllable; post-main syllable v is a suffix. T= /á/ high, /ā/ mid, /a/ (unmarked) low-level, /à/ low-falling. This paper will consider the pre-main syllable element symbolized cv above, which I will call presyllable (another possibility would have been the term 'minor syllable' used in much Mon-Khmer linguistic literature). [p. 343] ... Thus presyllables are phonologically dependent on their associated main syllables, not only in being unable to occur alone, but also in having their phonological realization partially determined by features of the main syllable: tonal features in the first type, vocalic features in the second. [p. 344] ... ʔa is the unmarked third person pronoun ... What I take to be the same item (or a closely related, homophonous item) occurs in various prefix-like constructions, listed below. In these it has only some of the phonological characteristics of a prefix: it is [p. 350] unstressed, at or near low-level pitch, and its vowel quality approaches [ə]. On the other hand at slower speech tempos it retains the vowel quality [a] and does not exhibit vowel harmony with the following syllable. [p. 351]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (13-page SEAlang scan, pp. 343-355, no text layer) and rendered scan pages 1, 2, 8, 9 (= printed pp. 343, 344, 350, 351) at 110 dpi to read against the scanned file. All three stitched passages are on the page as quoted: p. 343 'The Kayah Li* phonological word is the structure of those lexical items which are neither analyzeable compounds; truly polysyllabic morphemes.. This structure may be abbreviated as:' followed by the two-line diagram (t T t over c v C C V v; the quote linearizes it as '[t T t / cv CCV v]'), then 'Upper-case elements are required, and lower-case are optional.. CCV is main syllable; post-main syllable v is a suffix. T= /á/ high, /ā/ mid, /a/ (unmarked) low-level…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kayah Li is a tone language (four tones) with sesquisyllabic words: an optional reduced presyllable (minor syllable: C+schwa/copy vowel or ?i-, with restricted tones) precedes the full main syllable, which carries the contrastive tone and the stress; presyllables are unstressed and phonologically dependent on the following main syllable. Stress therefore falls on the (last) full/major syllable of the phonological word, i.e. a right-headed (iambic) pattern (Bennett 1995 abstract: 'consistent pattern of metrical right-headedness.. iambic foot structure.. major syllables and minor syllables'). Solnit 1997 p.17 / 2003 p.624 note that in disyllabic compounds such as be se 'face' the first element can be unstressed with vowel lowering (/bəse/), so the same right-headed reduction extends to compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by any opened source; Bennett 1995 abstract says Southeast Asian languages, Kayah Li included, 'lack the alternating patterns of multiple stress levels'.
new_statements.exceptions: The prefix-like ?a is only partly reduced (retains [a] and no vowel harmony at slower tempos); a rare suffix syllable (copy vowel with high-falling tone) follows the main syllable, so the stressed syllable is not always word-final; presyllable reduction is tempo/speech-style dependent (Solnit 1992 p.344, 2003 p.625; Bennett 1995).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (lexical item): presyllable + main syllable (+ suffix); observations in isolation/citation forms and connected speech; compounds mentioned only via the be se example. The stress statement is a passing observation about presyllables, not a formulated stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: All of Solnit's data (1992 paper, 1997 grammar, 2003 sketch) describe Eastern Kayah Li, Lower (kê kê) dialect, as spoken by refugees/settlers in Mae Hong Son province, Thailand (2003 p. 623: 'The language described in this chapter is the Lower variety'; 1992 fn.: Eastern dialect area, Mae Hong Son 1983-84, 1987-88) = east2342 [eky]. Bennett 1995 says only 'Kayah Li'; Bryant 1996 shows Bennett worked with both an Eastern (Khu Klawreh) and a Western (Khu Noah) speaker, so the dialect behind his metrical analysis is unverified (Western Kayah = kaya1317? / iso kyu, not checked). Bryant & Paulsen 1996 (examined, no stress) is Western Kayah Li [kyu], a different language.

new_statements.quote: Following Hayes 1994, I take stress to be abstract, realized structurally on the head syllables of prosodic constituents. The exponents of stress in Thai and Kayah Li are two syllable weight and tonality, two binary oppositions (which accounts for the lack of multiple stress levels). The close association of syllable weight with foot headship, plus a consistent pattern of metrical right-headedness, derives iambic foot structure, and forms the basis for the frequent distinction between major syllables and minor syllables.
new_statements.citation: Bennett, Jefferson Fraser. 1995. Metrical foot structure in Thai and Kayah Li: Optimality-theoretic studies in the prosody of two Southeast Asian languages. PhD, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
new_statements.locator: Abstract, paragraphs 1-2, on the IDEALS landing page https://www.ideals.illinois.edu/items/22377 (handle 2142/22242). The body (8,553,940 B;, 368,955 B) is Illinois-restricted: the page says 'This item is only available for download by members of the University of Illinois community', and both bitstream URLs (/items/22377/bitstreams/74983/object and /82418/object) could not be reached by automated download Access Denied.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: After tag-stripping, the Abstract block contains the quoted passage character-for-character: 'Following Hayes 1994, I take stress to be abstract, realized structurally on the head syllables of prosodic constituents. The exponents of stress in Thai and Kayah Li are two syllable weight and tonality, two binary oppositions (which accounts for the lack of multiple stress levels). The close association of syllable weight with foot headship, plus a consistent pattern of metrical right-headedness, derives iambic foot structure, and forms the basis for the frequent distinction between major syllables and minor syllables.' The same three sentences appear with identical wording in a second open copy…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Solnit 1992 statement (presyllable unstressed and phonologically dependent on the main syllable; tone language). Bennett adds the metrical analysis: right-headed iambic feet with the major syllable as head, stress cued by weight and tonality, no multiple stress levels, and style-dependent reduction. The full dissertation could not be opened, so section, page and any explicit word-level rule remain unverified; the 'open copy online' tag in READALL_TARGETS is wrong for this item (UIUC-login / ProQuest only).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the abstract only: Kayah Li (a tone language) has abstract stress realized as the head of a prosodic foot; feet are consistently right-headed (iambic), so the heavy, tone-bearing major syllable is the head and the preceding light minor syllable (presyllable) is unstressed. Stress is cued by syllable weight and tonality, both binary, so there are no multiple stress levels. Word-level placement beyond the major/minor-syllable distinction is not stated in the abstract.
new_statements.secondary_stress: The abstract says Southeast Asian languages 'generally lack the alternating patterns of multiple stress levels' and that the binary exponents of stress account 'for the lack of multiple stress levels' -- i.e. no secondary-stress level is reported.
new_statements.exceptions: Phonologically distinct speech styles are analysed as different constraint rankings: hyperarticulated speech preserves all underlying featural specifications, while 'hypoarticulated speech minimizes prosodic structure'. No lexical exceptions are mentioned in the abstract.
new_statements.identity_note: Bennett's abstract says only 'Kayah Li' with no dialect named. The catalog's Solnit 1992 data are explicitly Eastern Kayah Li (Lower dialect, Mae Hong Son province, Thailand); whether Bennett used the same (Solnit-derived) Eastern data could not be checked because the body of the dissertation is inaccessible.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on substance: the one work in this item (Bennett 1995, open only as the 24-page ProQuest preview) describes 'Kayah Li' as a tone language with binary stress realised as syllable weight + tonality in right-headed (iambic) feet, which matches the catalog's Eastern Kayah Li coding from Solnit 1992/1994 (tonal; unstressed dependent presyllable + toned main syllable). The conflict is one of IDENTITY, not content: Bennett's Kayah Li case study is explicitly Western Kayah Li (west2409; diss. pp. 1, 2, 4; Glottolog ref 14865 'Western Kayah [kyu]'), so the verified statement held by the project that credits Bennett 1995 to east2342 (taken from the IDEALS abstract, which says only 'Kayah Li') is attached to the wrong glottocode and should move to west2409; the east2342 record itself (Solnit) is unaffected.
